lesson.title: Which Comes First, Feeling or Physiology? Three Theories of Emotion
lesson.summary: Psychologists have proposed several historically competing explanations for how emotion arises from physiological arousal and cognitive interpretation, with the James-Lange, Cannon-Bard, and Schachter-Singer theories marking three influential, and different, answers developed in sequence.
lesson.body:
The question of what causes what in emotion, does the body react first and the felt emotion follow, or does the feeling come first and the body simply follow along, is a good example of why psychology insists on testable, falsifiable claims rather than accepting a single intuitive answer. Three major theories, developed across roughly a century, each proposed a different, testable account of the relationship between bodily arousal and subjective feeling, and each responded to real limitations in the theory before it.

The James-Lange theory, associated with William James and Carl Lange working independently in the late 1800s, proposed that physiological arousal comes first and the subjective experience of emotion follows from, and is caused by, our perception of that bodily response. In this view, we do not tremble because we feel afraid, we feel afraid because we notice ourselves trembling, the specific pattern of bodily reaction is what generates the specific emotion experienced.

The Cannon-Bard theory developed largely as a critique of James-Lange. Physiologist Walter Cannon, and later Philip Bard, argued that bodily arousal and the subjective feeling of an emotion are triggered at essentially the same time and somewhat independently of each other by the same underlying brain activity, rather than one causing the other. Part of Cannon's argument rested on the observation that very different emotions can produce strikingly similar patterns of physiological arousal, which made it hard to see how the body's reaction alone, without some separate emotional response occurring in parallel, could account for the distinct emotions people actually report feeling.

That debate concerned physiological arousal in fairly broad terms, and later research pushed further into the specific neural and chemical detail of that arousal, connecting back to neurotransmitters and stress hormones such as epinephrine. That more detailed view of arousal set the stage for the Schachter-Singer two-factor theory, which proposed that emotion requires two ingredients together, physiological arousal, plus a cognitive label the person applies to explain that arousal, drawn from the surrounding situation. The same underlying arousal, given a different situational label, was proposed to produce a different felt emotion.

The theory's classic support comes from a well known 1962 study by Schachter and Singer, in which participants were injected with epinephrine, some were accurately told what physical effects to expect from it and some were not, and all were then placed alongside a confederate who behaved either euphorically or angrily. Participants who had not been told what to expect from their own arousal were more likely to adopt an emotional state matching the confederate's behavior, apparently searching their situation for a plausible explanation of arousal they could not otherwise account for.

It is worth being clear that these three theories are best understood as a historical sequence of competing explanations, each built to address a gap in the one before it, rather than as a single settled account that current psychologists all agree on. Later work, including theories emphasizing the role of cognitive appraisal in generating emotion in the first place, has continued to refine and complicate the picture further, and the relationship between physiology and cognition in emotion remains an active area of research. Even so, the vocabulary these three classic theories introduced, arousal causing feeling, arousal and feeling arising together, and arousal combined with cognitive labeling, remains the essential starting point for thinking about where emotion actually comes from.
